implementation.portedInvariant: a path is resolved by walking its link chain one hop at a time under a 64-hop bound, refusing a chain that is too long, loops, has an unreadable ancestor or lands on a network filesystem, and the resolution carries the hops and a dev/ino/ctime/size identity that a read or an overwrite can check
ownedDecisions: The bound stays at 64 hops, which is deliberately not the kernel's own limit, so a chain between the two is refused here by name rather than by the kernel with a bare ELOOP.
A loop is refused with the same ELOOP code rather than falling back to a direct realpath, because that fallback exists to serve an unreadable-ancestry policy this runtime does not have.
The identity is the recovered dev/ino/ctimeMs triple with the byte length added, checked against the open handle for a read and against a re-stat before an overwrite.
The unreadable-ancestry verdict is a refusal rather than a marker, because this runtime has no policy that would treat an unverified ancestor as usable.
Network landings are refused by reading the filesystem type of the landing path, since the recovered predicates live in an imported path-classification module and cover Windows device and UNC forms.

identity.independentOfflineRebuild: fresh directory, source bundle of 205 files, npm ci --ignore-scripts --offline, check and build, identical merged digest

regressions: The full suite covers the file tools, media reads, notebooks and every session path that shares the confinement helper. One regression appeared during the port and was fixed before the record was written: the read stream was built with autoClose disabled and its descriptor was then closed in the same finally block, which double-closed it and surfaced as EBADF in the read and session-storage suites. The stream now owns the descriptor and only the pre-stream failure path closes it by hand. No previously passing case changed.
limitations: The network-landing refusal is exercised through an injected filesystem-type reader, so the refusal is verified but nothing is claimed about a real network mount.

Identity timestamps are only as fine as the filesystem records them: APFS on this host advances ctime in whole seconds, so a same-size in-place rewrite inside one tick is not detected. The byte length covers the size-changing case regardless of the clock.
The network magic-number list can only be wrong by omission; an exotic network filesystem missing from it is not refused.
